paragraphs: One of the proofs for the soundness of naẓar and istidlāl is the following: knowledge must either (i) arise only by way of direct observation (mushāhada), or (ii) only by way of necessity (ḍarūra), or (iii) only by way of report (akhbār). The unsoundness of all three positions has been demonstrated in the preceding babs; and once those three are eliminated, it follows necessarily that knowledge arises by naẓar and istidlāl.[{2}] What further refutes the opponent who claims that "nothing is known by istidlāl or naẓar" is that, if his thesis were correct, it would not be obligatory to infer a writer from a written text, or a striker from one struck, or a killer from one killed, or a builder from a building. Yet [imagine] a man who goes out into the desert and sees no constructed palace there, and then returns and finds a palace standing. […it would be absurd to deny…] that it had come into being in this place after not having been there […]; the inference to a builder [is necessary],[{3}] for we find that what is built is never built except by a builder. We also find the bricks, the mortar, and the plaster present in some other location before the palace was built — and even if the palace had been prefabricated in another place, then transported and assembled here, that itself is a concession to something the speaker did not observe. Whatever is not by mushāhada and not by iḍṭirār (i.e. not by direct observation and not by immediate compulsion of ʿilm ḍarūrī), is therefore by istidlāl. And if abandoning naẓar and istidlāl leads to self-imposed ignorance (al-tajāhul) — and tajāhul is universally condemned and not praiseworthy — then what the opponent rejects, namely naẓar, is what is in fact obligatory.[{4}]

A further proof that naẓar and baḥth are constitutive of the rational faculty in all mankind is this: there is no human being who, upon being called "ignorant!" (yā jāhil), accepts the label and is at peace with it. Rather, he resents it, rejects it, takes offense, and repels it from himself by whatever means he has at his disposal. This is one of the clearest signs that the repudiation of ignorance is constitutive of the human intellect, intrinsic to the self. And nothing repels ignorance except baḥth and naẓar, which proceed by discrimination (tamyīz) and analogy (qiyās). It is therefore established that the obligation of inquiry and reflection is constitutive of every human intellect.[{5}]

A further argument for the obligation of baḥth and naẓar in matters where the religions disagree: we find that the religions disagree on a great many questions, and that each side accuses the others of error. Their disagreement cannot, however, be such that all of them are right, nor such that all of them are wrong. It cannot be that all of them are wrong, since were that the case, the truth would lie outside religion altogether; once one position is shown to be corrupt, its contradictory must hold — for it is impossible for a thing and its contradictory both to be false (just as it is impossible for them both to be true), since if the ruling is not "lawful," it must be "forbidden." It therefore remains that some of the religions are right and some wrong; and discrimination between truth and falsehood is universally obligatory upon all rational creatures by way of al-maʿqūl (the rational faculty) and command together.[{6}] […] And the very act of demanding the proof of truth — of asking the opponent for his ḥujja — is itself a concession to the obligation of naẓar and baḥth, and thereby an annulment of the opponent's own denial of naẓar and baḥth.[{7}] ---
